C005.subject: Economic growth
C005.object: under standard neoclassical growth models with fixed natural resource inputs, no technological change, and no substitution elasticity between capital and natural resources above 1
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Economic growth under standard neoclassical growth models with fixed natural resource inputs, no technological change, and no substitution elasticity between capital and natural resources above 1]

[PATH:theoretical] Dasgupta, P. & Heal, G. (1974). 'The Optimal Depletion of Exhaustible Resources.' Review of Economic Studies, 41, 3-28. — This foundational paper analytically derives conditions for sustainable consumption in neoclassical growth models with exhaustible resources. It directly addresses whether perpetual growth is possible when substitution elasticity between capital and natural resources is less than or equal to 1, and thus can confirm or refute the mathematical impossibility claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Stiglitz, J. (1974). 'Growth with Exhaustible Natural Resources: Efficient and Optimal Growth Paths.' Review of Economic Studies, 41, 123-137. — Stiglitz's work provides a rigorous mathematical framework showing that under certain conditions (e.g., elasticity of substitution greater than 1, or sufficient technical change), growth can be sustained. This paper is essential for verifying whether the hypothesis holds when substitution elasticity is exactly at or below 1, and for understanding the boundary cases.

[PATH:theoretical] Acemoglu, D. (2003). 'Labor- and Capital-Augmenting Technical Change.' Journal of the European Economic Association, 1(1), 1-37. — This paper extends neoclassical growth models to include directed technical change, which can effectively raise the substitution elasticity between capital and natural resources. It provides a theoretical basis to test whether the hypothesis's 'no technological change' assumption is crucial, and whether induced innovation could circumvent the impossibility result.

scope.domain: theoretical resource-constrained scenarios with low substitution elasticity

C006.subject: Economic growth
C006.predicate: is not universal but is constrained to countries that
C006.object: achieved a minimum threshold of institutional stability (e.g., a Polity IV score above 0) prior to 1950
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Economic growth achieved a minimum threshold of institutional stability (e.g., a Polity IV score above 0) prior to 1950]

[PATH:empirical] Polity IV dataset (annual polity scores for all countries, 1800-2018) combined with Maddison Project Database (real GDP per capita, 1820-2018) — Directly tests the hypothesis by coding a binary threshold (Polity > 0 before 1950) and comparing post-war (1945-1970) GDP growth rates between countries that met vs. did not meet the threshold, controlling for other growth determinants.

[PATH:literature] Acemoglu, D., Johnson, S., & Robinson, J. A. (2001). 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation.' American Economic Review, 91(5), 1369-1401. — Establishes the causal role of early institutional stability (measured by constraints on executives, similar to Polity) on long-run economic development, providing a theoretical and empirical foundation for the hypothesis that pre-1950 institutional thresholds matter for post-war growth.

[PATH:empirical] Historical institutional stability indices (e.g., V-Dem's liberal democracy index, 1789-2020) and panel regressions with country and decade fixed effects — Allows testing the robustness of the Polity IV threshold by using alternative measures of institutional stability, and examining whether the 1950 cutoff is arbitrary or reflects a genuine structural break in the relationship between institutions and growth.

scope.domain: observed post-war global GDP time series
